actions.name: PHQ-9 depression screen (reviewed from referral)
actions.result: PHQ-9 total score 19/27 (moderately severe depression). Positive on items for sleep disturbance, fatigue, appetite/weight change, feelings of failure/guilt, and the self-harm item ('thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself') scored as 1 (several days).

actions.name: Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) screening
actions.result: No C-SSRS on file. The screener is completed by asking the patient its questions directly during the interview; record her answers as she gives them. PCP referral note documents only a brief denial of specific plan/intent during the office visit, without a full passive-ideation inquiry. No history of suicide attempts is documented anywhere in the record.

actions.name: Mental status examination via video
actions.result: Alert, cooperative, well-groomed older woman. Speech soft, slow, decreased spontaneity. Mood 'tired, kind of empty.' Affect restricted, congruent, occasionally tearful. Thought process linear, no flight of ideas. Thought content: guilt-laden ruminations, no delusions; thoughts of death or self-harm to be assessed by direct questioning. No hallucinations reported or observed. Cognition grossly intact on bedside screening. Insight and judgment intact; help-seeking appropriate.

actions.name: Cognitive screening (Mini-Cog, performed by phone/video)
actions.result: 3-word recall 3/3, clock draw accurately placed by patient and described verbally, scored normal. No evidence of dementia or delirium.

actions.name: Review PCP referral note
actions.result: Referral letter from primary care: widow at 4 months, progressive low mood, anhedonia, 6 kg (13 lb) weight loss over 3 months, early morning awakening, guilt. PHQ-9 administered in clinic scored 19. TSH checked given fatigue, was normal. Patient referred for psychiatric evaluation of major depressive episode versus complicated grief.

actions.name: Review recent thyroid function tests (TSH, free T4)
actions.result: TSH 2.1 mIU/L (reference 0.4-4.0), Free T4 1.1 ng/dL (reference 0.8-1.8) drawn 3 weeks ago — both within normal range, thyroid replacement adequately dosed.

actions.name: Review complete blood count and metabolic panel
actions.result: CBC and comprehensive metabolic panel from 3 weeks ago within normal limits; no anemia, normal renal and hepatic function, normal electrolytes and glucose.

actions.name: Review home blood pressure and weight log
actions.result: Home BP log over past month ranges 118-132/70-80 mmHg, stable on amlodipine. Weight trend shows 6 kg loss over 3 months, now stabilizing with no further loss in last 2 weeks per patient's bathroom scale log.

actions.name: Review current medication list and refill history
actions.result: Levothyroxine 75 mcg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, both filled on schedule monthly. No psychiatric medications on list. Pharmacy refill history shows amlodipine refilled 2 weeks late last fill (consistent with patient's report of occasional missed doses amid grief).

actions.name: Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT-C), administered verbally
actions.result: Score 4/12 (frequency 4 or more times a week = 4; typical quantity 1-2 drinks = 0; six or more drinks on one occasion never = 0). This is at or above the positive-screen cutoff of 3 for women, so it is a positive screen that warrants further assessment. Clinically it reflects new nightly low-quantity use to get to sleep rather than an established alcohol use disorder, but it needs discussion given its new onset and the interaction risk with any sedating medication.

actions.name: Camera inspection of general appearance and self-care
actions.result: Patient appropriately dressed in a cardigan, hair neatly combed, home appears tidy with photographs visible in background including a wedding photo. No evidence of self-neglect.

actions.name: Review grief/bereavement screening tools in chart
actions.result: No prior documentation of a formal bereavement inventory; PCP note described symptoms meeting depressive syndrome criteria rather than uncomplicated grief, given pervasive low mood, anhedonia beyond missing husband specifically, and neurovegetative symptoms persisting most of every day.

actions.name: Lethal means access and safety planning assessment
actions.result: Nothing about firearms or stored medications is documented in the record. Lethal-means access can only be established by asking the patient directly; build the safety plan with her from what she tells you.

actions.name: Sleep pattern and insomnia assessment
actions.result: Reports early morning awakening around 3:30-4:00 AM most nights, unable to return to sleep, with daytime fatigue. Uses sherry most nights attempting to fall asleep initially but wakes early regardless.

No acute safety concerns identified in brief office screen but recommend formal psychiatric evaluation given severity and endorsement of item 9. objectives.text: Elicit a longitudinal depression history including neurovegetative symptoms, anhedonia, and guilt, and distinguish major depressive episode from uncomplicated grief in the context of recent bereavement.
Conduct a thorough, direct suicide risk assessment including passive ideation, plan, intent, protective factors, and access to lethal means, and translate findings into a safety plan.
Screen for and characterize a new, clinically relevant pattern of alcohol use as self-medication for insomnia, and factor this into treatment planning.
Identify and rule out a medical/endocrine contributor to the mood presentation, and recognize the mismatch between the patient's belief about her thyroid and the actual lab trend.
Perform a bedside mental status and cognitive screen appropriate to a telehealth visit and integrate findings into a biopsychosocial formulation.

Formulate a stepwise treatment plan within psychiatric scope: antidepressant initiation, psychotherapy referral, level-of-care decision given risk, and appropriate follow-up interval, while recognizing when primary care or emergency services involvement is needed.

answerKey.primaryProblem: Major depressive episode (moderately severe, PHQ-9 19) precipitated by spousal bereavement at 4 months, with passive suicidal ideation and identified access to lethal means, superimposed on normal grief but distinguished by pervasive anhedonia, guilt, and neurovegetative symptoms beyond the index loss.
differential: Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderately severe
Uncomplicated/normal bereavement (grief reaction) - less likely given pervasiveness of anhedonia beyond missing husband, persistent guilt, and functional impairment at 4 months
Persistent complex bereavement disorder / prolonged grief disorder - consider but mood symptoms and anhedonia extend beyond grief-specific content
Hypothyroidism-related mood/fatigue symptoms - ruled out by current normal TSH/free T4
Alcohol use disorder - AUDIT-C positive screen (4/12) without features of dependence; new nightly use for self-medicated insomnia is a modifiable risk factor
Adjustment disorder with depressed mood - less likely given symptom severity and duration meeting full MDE criteria
keyFindings: 4 months since husband's death with anhedonia extending beyond grief (stopped reading group and choir)
6 kg unintentional weight loss over 3 months, now stabilizing
Early morning awakening around 3:30-4:00 AM nightly
Passive death wish ('wish I wouldn't wake up') elicited only after rapport-building and a direct question; no plan or intent
Access to lethal means in home: husband's leftover oxycodone (~20 tablets) and his unlocked hunting rifle
New nightly alcohol use (2 glasses sherry) for sleep, AUDIT-C 4/12 (positive screen for women), clinically relevant given insomnia and future sedative interaction risk
TSH/free T4 normal, ruling out hypothyroid contribution despite patient's belief that her thyroid 'might be acting up again'
Protective factors: strong faith community, close relationship with grandchildren, help-seeking behavior, no prior attempts
Mental status exam: linear thought process, intact insight/judgment, normal cognitive screen
plan: Initiate an SSRI (e.g., sertraline 25-50 mg daily, titrating as tolerated) given efficacy in late-life depression and favorable interaction profile; avoid medications that interact adversely with evening alcohol use until use is reduced
Arrange same-day or next-day removal of husband's unused oxycodone and the hunting rifle from the home by son or other trusted family member; document means restriction counseling
Establish a collaborative safety plan with the patient including warning signs, coping strategies, identified support person (son), and crisis line/ER instructions if ideation worsens
Refer to psychotherapy: grief-focused therapy and/or cognitive behavioral therapy for late-life depression; consider interpersonal therapy given the clear interpersonal loss trigger
Counsel on reducing nightly alcohol use for sleep; provide sleep hygiene education and address insomnia as a treatment target, reassessing need for a non-sedative approach as mood improves
Close follow-up within 1-2 weeks to reassess suicide risk and medication tolerability given moderate risk stratification; do not wait the standard 4-6 week follow-up interval given risk level
Coordinate with PCP regarding thyroid monitoring continuity and overall medical care; this role does not need to independently manage amlodipine/levothyroxine but should communicate findings

If at any point active suicidal ideation, intent, or plan emerges, escalate immediately to emergency evaluation (crisis line, mobile crisis team, or emergency department) rather than managing solely outpatient
redFlags: Passive suicidal ideation with identified in-home access to a firearm and an opioid medication constitutes a safety-relevant combination requiring explicit means-restriction counseling regardless of 'no plan/no intent' reassurance
Significant unintentional weight loss (6 kg/13 lb) in an older adult always warrants consideration of a general medical workup, already appropriately initiated by PCP
New-onset nightly alcohol use in an older widow self-medicating insomnia can escalate and complicates future pharmacotherapy and sedative-hypnotic use
Any emergence of active ideation, intent, plan, or acute agitation during follow-up should trigger immediate escalation to emergency services rather than routine outpatient management
educationPoints: Distinguishing normal grief from major depressive disorder in bereavement: pervasive and persistent anhedonia (not limited to thoughts of the deceased), excessive/inappropriate guilt beyond the circumstances of the death, and significant functional impairment favor a depressive episode warranting treatment.

Passive suicidal ideation ('I wish I wouldn't wake up') must be actively and directly elicited with a warm, nonjudgmental approach, especially in reserved or stoic patients who may minimize distress or feel they are 'wasting the doctor's time.'

Lethal means counseling (asking specifically about firearms and medications in the home) is a core, evidence-based component of suicide risk reduction and should be concrete and action-oriented (who removes it, when).
Older adults are at elevated risk for completed suicide despite often reporting only passive ideation, making risk stratification and close follow-up especially important in this age group.
New or escalating alcohol use as self-treatment for insomnia in grief/depression is common and should be screened for explicitly, as it affects both diagnosis and safe prescribing.

facts.chart: Patient referred by PCP for evaluation of low mood and related symptoms since husband's death 4 months ago.
facts.says: My doctor thought I should talk to someone because I haven't been myself since my husband passed. I feel a little silly being here, honestly.

facts.chart: Describes mood as low, flat, 'empty' most of each day for approximately 3 months.
facts.says: Most days I just feel... tired and empty. Not sad exactly, more like hollowed out.

facts.chart: Anhedonia: stopped attending weekly reading group and church choir, activities previously enjoyed for over a decade.
facts.says: I used to love my Tuesday reading group and singing in the choir. I haven't gone in weeks. I just can't make myself care about it anymore.

facts.chart: Early morning awakening around 3:30-4:00 AM nightly, unable to return to sleep, for the past 2-3 months.
facts.says: I wake up at four in the morning like clockwork and just lie there until it's light out. I used to sleep straight through.

facts.chart: Decreased appetite with 6 kg (13 lb) unintentional weight loss over 3 months, now stabilizing.
facts.says: I just don't have much of an appetite anymore. My daughter noticed my clothes were getting loose on me.

facts.chart: Prominent guilt that she 'should have noticed' her husband's illness sooner, feels she failed him.
facts.says: I keep thinking, I was his wife for 46 years, how did I not see he was so sick? I feel like I failed him.

facts.chart: Reports fatigue and some difficulty concentrating, particularly with reading, which contributes to withdrawal from reading group.
facts.says: I try to read and my mind just wanders. I used to finish a book in two days, now I can't get through a chapter.

facts.chart: Endorses passive death wish: thoughts that she would rather not wake up in the morning. No active suicidal ideation.
facts.says: Some mornings when I wake up at four, I think... I wish I just wouldn't wake up at all. It's not that I'd do anything, I just feel so tired of feeling this way.

facts.chart: Denies any specific plan, method, or intent to end her life. Denies prior suicide attempts.
facts.says: Oh no, I wouldn't do anything to hurt myself. I just mean I feel so worn out sometimes. I've never tried anything like that.

facts.chart: Confirms husband's unused oxycodone prescription (approximately 20 tablets) and his hunting rifle remain unlocked in the house.
facts.says: His pain pills from the hospice are still in the medicine cabinet, I never got around to throwing them out. And his rifle is still in the hall closet where he always kept it.

facts.chart: Identifies her Christian faith and relationship with grandchildren as strong protective factors and reasons to live.
facts.says: My faith means a lot to me, and I have four grandchildren who need their grandmother around. That keeps me going, truly.

facts.chart: Son lives 20 minutes away and visits weekly; agreeable to being contacted as a safety resource.
facts.says: My son Mark comes by most Sundays. He'd come sooner if I asked him to.

facts.chart: Agreeable to having son remove the oxycodone and rifle from the home this week once risk discussed.
facts.says: If you think it's a good idea, I suppose I could have Mark take those things when he's over this weekend. I hadn't really thought about it that way.

facts.chart: New-onset nightly alcohol use: 2 glasses of sherry most evenings for approximately 2 months, intended to help with sleep onset.
facts.says: I started having a little sherry in the evening, maybe two small glasses, just to help me settle down and fall asleep. I never used to drink like that.

facts.chart: Denies any history of problematic alcohol use prior to husband's death; occasional wine at holidays only.
facts.says: Before all this, I'd maybe have a glass of wine at Christmas. This is new for me.

facts.chart: Reports the sherry helps her fall asleep initially but does not prevent early morning awakening.
facts.says: It helps me drift off, but I still wake up at four no matter what. So I'm not sure it's even helping anymore.

facts.chart: Patient attributes some fatigue to possible thyroid problem; believes her thyroid medication 'might need adjusting' though unaware of recent normal labs.
facts.says: I wonder if it's my thyroid acting up again, I take a pill for that, maybe the dose needs changing.

facts.chart: Reports taking levothyroxine and amlodipine 'every day without missing,' though pharmacy refill history shows a 2-week-late amlodipine refill last cycle.
facts.says: Oh, I take my pills every single day, I never miss. I'm very careful about that.

facts.chart: Denies auditory or visual hallucinations, denies feeling that others are watching or targeting her.
facts.says: No, I don't hear or see anything that isn't there. Nothing like that.

facts.chart: Denies any past episodes of elevated mood, decreased need for sleep with high energy, or impulsive spending; no personal or family history of bipolar disorder.
facts.says: No, I've never had spells where I felt wonderful and didn't need sleep or went on spending sprees. Nothing like that ever.

facts.chart: Denies significant memory loss, getting lost, or difficulty managing finances/medications beyond concentration difficulty attributed to mood.
facts.says: My memory's fine, I think, I just have trouble focusing when I try to read.

facts.chart: Reports spending most days alone at home; limited structured activity since withdrawing from choir and reading group.
facts.says: Most days I just putter around the house. It's quiet. Too quiet, really.

facts.chart: Expresses hope to 'feel like herself again' and eventually return to choir; open to trying medication if recommended but anxious about side effects.
facts.says: I'd like to feel like myself again, maybe get back to the choir someday. I'm a little nervous about pills though, I've heard they can change you.

facts.chart: Open to talking with a counselor or grief support group if recommended, though unfamiliar with what therapy involves.
facts.says: I've never done anything like counseling before, but if you think it would help, I'm willing to try.

facts.chart: Married 46 years; describes husband as her 'best friend' and primary daily companion, especially after retirement.
facts.says: We were married 46 years. He was my best friend, really, especially once we both retired.

facts.chart: Retired librarian; worked at the town library for over 30 years before retiring.
facts.says: I was the town librarian for over thirty years. I loved that job.

facts.chart: Has a daughter who lives out of state and calls weekly; son Mark is the nearer, more involved support.
facts.says: My daughter calls me every week from Ohio, but she's far away. Mark's the one close by.

facts.chart: Denies any history of tobacco or other substance use.
facts.says: I've never smoked, never touched drugs, nothing like that.

facts.chart: Denies any prior episodes of depression, anxiety disorder, or psychiatric treatment/hospitalization before this episode.
facts.says: I've never had anything like this before, never seen anyone for my nerves or anything like that.

facts.chart: Reports a maternal aunt who 'had a hard time with her nerves' and was hospitalized once decades ago, details unclear; no known family suicide history.
facts.says: My aunt on my mother's side had some kind of breakdown once, a long time ago, they put her in a hospital for it. I don't really know the details.

facts.chart: Reports PCP briefly asked about self-harm during the referral visit and she said she had no plan at that time, consistent with chart documentation.
facts.says: The doctor did ask me something about hurting myself at that visit, and I told her no, I wouldn't do that. It wasn't a long conversation though.

facts.chart: Expresses embarrassment and apology about 'taking up the doctor's time' for what she perceives as a minor issue.
facts.says: I feel bad taking up your time with this. I'm sure you have patients who need you more than I do.

facts.chart: Reports symptoms began gradually within the first month after husband's death and have progressively worsened rather than improved over the following 3 months.
facts.says: At first I thought it was just normal grieving, but instead of getting a little easier like people said it would, it's actually gotten harder.

facts.chart: Drinks 1 cup of decaffeinated coffee each morning; denies excessive caffeine intake.
facts.says: Just one cup of decaf in the morning, that's my habit, has been for years.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes her fatigue and low mood might be due to her thyroid medication needing adjustment.
mismatches.recordEvidence: TSH 2.1 mIU/L and Free T4 1.1 ng/dL, both within normal reference range, drawn 3 weeks ago, indicating adequately dosed thyroid replacement.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients commonly attribute depressive neurovegetative symptoms (fatigue, weight change) to a familiar medical diagnosis like thyroid disease. Clinicians should verify with current labs rather than assume the patient's self-attribution is correct, while still ruling out organic contributors appropriately.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient states she takes her levothyroxine and amlodipine every day without ever missing a dose.
mismatches.recordEvidence: Medication list/refill history shows amlodipine was refilled 2 weeks later than the due date on the most recent fill cycle.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Self-reported adherence is often overestimated, especially under the stress of grief and depression; cross-checking refill history can reveal gaps that the patient may not consciously recognize or may minimize, and this should be explored gently rather than confrontationally.

patient.name: Eleanor Whitfield
patient.appearance: An older woman with neatly combed white hair, wearing a buttoned cardigan, seated in a tidy living room with a wedding photograph visible on a shelf behind her. Her posture is slightly slumped, her expression tired and occasionally tearful, and she speaks slowly and softly, pausing often as if choosing her words carefully.

persona.personality: Reserved, polite, and self-effacing; a lifelong caretaker-type who is more comfortable asking about others than talking about herself.
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks softly and slowly, often apologizes for 'taking up time,' answers questions honestly but needs gentle encouragement to go beyond surface-level answers, especially on sensitive topics.
persona.emotionalState: Fatigued, subdued, intermittently tearful, with underlying guilt and shame about her symptoms and about seeking help.
persona.background: Worked as the town librarian for over 30 years before retiring at 65. Married to her husband Walter for 46 years; he died of pancreatic cancer four months ago after a brief illness. They have two adult children: a son Mark who lives nearby and a daughter in Ohio. Eleanor has been active in her church choir and a weekly reading group for over a decade, both of which she has stopped attending since the loss.
speechExamples: I feel a little silly being here, honestly, I'm sure you have patients who need you more.
Most days I just feel... tired and empty. Not sad exactly, more like hollowed out.
I keep thinking, I was his wife for 46 years, how did I not see he was so sick?
Some mornings when I wake up at four, I think, I wish I just wouldn't wake up at all.
If you think it's a good idea, I suppose I could have Mark take those things when he's over this weekend.
concerns: Worried she is 'wasting the doctor's time' with what she sees as ordinary grief.
Concerned that medication might 'change who she is.'
Uncertain whether what she's feeling is normal grief or something more.
Embarrassed about the new drinking habit and about still having her husband's medication and rifle in the house.

scenario.studentBrief: You are a psychiatry resident conducting a telehealth intake evaluation for Eleanor Whitfield, a 72-year-old woman referred by her primary care physician for evaluation of low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, poor sleep, and weight loss since her husband's death 4 months ago. Conduct a thorough psychiatric interview, mental status exam, and risk assessment, and formulate a diagnosis and treatment plan.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Low mood, loss of interest in previously enjoyed activities, poor sleep, and weight loss since her husband's death 4 months ago, referred by PCP for psychiatric evaluation.
scenario.openingLine: My doctor thought I should talk to someone because I haven't been myself since my husband passed. I feel a little silly being here, honestly.
tasks: Take a focused psychiatric history of the presenting concern and explore the timeline and nature of symptoms since the loss
Screen for contributing factors including substance use and review relevant medical history and chart data with the patient
Perform a telehealth-appropriate mental status exam and brief cognitive screen
Formulate a diagnosis and agree on a treatment plan with appropriate follow-up

profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in her living room in a small town in Vermont
profile.summary: A 72-year-old recently widowed retired librarian is referred by her primary care physician for evaluation of a moderately severe depressive episode (PHQ-9 19) marked by anhedonia, guilt, weight loss, and early morning awakening. The case centers on eliciting passive suicidal ideation and lethal means access (opioids and a firearm in the home) through rapport-building, screening a new self-medicating alcohol pattern, and distinguishing major depression from normal grief while reconciling two patient-chart mismatches (thyroid belief vs. normal labs; reported perfect adherence vs. a late refill).
profile.title: Depression and Passive Suicidal Ideation in a Recently Widowed Older Woman
